planting.note: Plant container or bare-root divisions in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil; site where its vigorous underground runners are welcome, or install a root barrier to contain spread.

directions: This Rosaceae relative of mountain ash carries deep green, odd-pinnate compound leaves on a coarse, multi-stemmed frame, giving it a fern-like texture unusual among flowering shrubs. Dense, pyramidal plumes of tiny white flowers, often 6 to 10 inches long, cover the branch tips from early to midsummer and age to attractive tan seed clusters. It colonizes readily by root suckers, especially in loose soil, so it is best used as a naturalizing mass on a slope or bank rather than a tidy foundation planting. Though foliage color is strongest in full sun, the species performs well in partial shade and tolerates poor or lime-rich soils with little fuss once established.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in average, medium-moisture soil; this selection suckers far less aggressively than the species so it needs little root management once sited.

directions: A compact sport of Ural false spirea, 'Sem' emerges each spring in shades of shrimp-pink and bronze before the pinnate foliage matures to lime-green and finally deep green by summer, giving three seasons of foliage interest on one plant. Dense terminal panicles of small white flowers open in early summer above the colorful leaves, drawing bees and other pollinators. It holds a much tighter, rounded habit than the straight species and spreads far less by suckering, making it workable near a shaded border or woodland edge instead of only wild, naturalized ground. Give it full sun to partial shade and an occasional hard cutback in late winter to refresh size and flower display.

planting.note: Plant small container specimens in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in bright to partial shade; this East Asian species is still frequently sold under its older name, Gaultheria miqueliana.

directions: A dense, twiggy dwarf shrub native to Japan and nearby East Asia, this wintergreen relative forms a low, spreading mound of small rounded leaves on new growth that emerges bright pinkish-red before hardening to glossy green. Clusters of tiny white, urn-shaped flowers open in summer and give way to fleshy white-to-pink berries that persist into fall. It thrives as a woodland-edge groundcover in bright or partial shade and needs consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil to perform well, resenting both drought and heavy clay. Use it at the front of a shaded border or tucked among taller shade shrubs where its fine texture and berry display can be appreciated up close.
sources: Oregon State University Landscape Plants Database

planting.note: Plant in spring in lime-free, humus-rich, evenly moist soil in shade to semi-shade; mulch with leaf litter to mimic its native Himalayan woodland floor.

directions: Native to the eastern Himalaya and adjacent mountains of southwestern China and northern Myanmar, this creeping, semi-erect evergreen forms a dense, compact mat of bright green, rounded leaves reminiscent of a pyrola. Small, scented white flowers, occasionally blushed pink, open in late spring to early summer and are followed by small fleshy fruit. It demands a cool, humus-rich, acidic, lime-free soil that never fully dries out, and performs best tucked into shade to semi-shade where taller shrubs shelter it from drying wind and sun. Its low mat-forming habit makes it a useful living mulch at the base of larger rhododendrons, pieris, or other acid-loving woodland shrubs.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, light, acidic, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this southeastern Tibetan species spreads gently by suckers once established.

directions: Collected from southeastern Tibet, this spreading evergreen shrub carries narrow, glossy dark green leaves and makes an airy, suckering thicket in the woodland garden over time. Nodding flowers in shades of pink and white appear in spring and summer, followed by showy blue fruit that stands out against the foliage into fall. It is happiest in partial to full shade on light, moisture-retentive, acidic soil, and struggles in hot, exposed sites with heavy or alkaline ground. Site it among rhododendrons or other broadleaf evergreens where its fruit display and fine foliage texture can fill the shaded middle layer of a planting.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in lime-free, humus-rich, peaty or sandy loam amended with leaf mold, in partial to full shade; this slow-growing Japanese species is far less commonly offered than fontanesiana, axillaris, or keiskei types.

directions: Native to the mountain woodlands of Japan, this slow-growing, upright member of the heath family carries leathery, oblong leaves with conspicuous veining on a more erect frame than the familiar fontanesiana and axillaris doghobbles. Drooping, terminal racemes of small white-to-pink flowers open in summer, later than most cultivated leucothoes, extending bloom interest into the shade garden's quieter season. In cold climates the foliage can drop or take on russet tones in fall, blurring the line between deciduous and evergreen depending on the winter. It needs a lime-free, consistently moist, humus-rich soil and performs best tucked into partial to full shade sheltered from drying wind, making it a specimen choice for collectors building out a woodland leucothoe collection.
sources: Oregon State University Landscape Plants Database
